newsitem.title: GERMANY: No let-up in rising catastrophe trend - Munich Re.
newsitem.headline: No let-up in rising catastrophe trend - Munich Re.

text.p: Despite a relatively stable year for floods, hurricanes and other natural disasters in 1996, the global trend toward increased incidence of catastrophes is continuing, Munich Re said on Wednesday.
In a regular report on global disasters, the world's largest reinsurer said its geoscientists still saw a trend toward "ever-increasing losses with ever-increasing costs."

In addition, earth temperatures are continuing to rise, making 1996 one of the 10 warmest years since global metereological records began 150 years ago. All 10 of those record years have occured since 1980.
"Mankind will increasingly be confronted with new extreme metereological conditions," Munich Re said.

"The people in the regions affected will not have the experience with such extreme conditions and will therefore not have taken appropriate preventive action. This will inevitably lead to the occurrence of catastrophes."

Total economic losses from catastrophes in 1996 were $60 billion, while insured losses were well below those of previous years at $9 billion, mainly due to low insurance density in the areas affected.
The biggest damage by far was caused by extreme flooding along China's Yangtse river, which lasted from June through August, killed 2,700 people and made two million homeless.
The cost of the disaster was more than $20 billion.
